questions.q: The pure wealth-maximisation objective preferred over profit maximisation primarily because it:
o: Considers timing, risk and magnitude of cash flows and avoids myopic accounting profit
questions.why: Wealth maximisation uses discounted cash flows (timing+risk) and market value; profit maximisation is accounting-based, ambiguous in timing and ignores risk.

questions.q: Under the Companies Act CSR provisions tested in the corporate-strategy chapter, companies meeting the prescribed thresholds must spend at least what share of average net profits (computed per the Act) in the immediately preceding three financial years?

questions.why: Beta (systematic) cannot be diversified; idiosyncratic risk averages away in large portfolios.

questions.q: A 5% one-day VaR of Rs 2 crore on a portfolio means:
o: On 5 of every 100 days (approx), the one-day loss EXCEEDS Rs 2 crore
5% of portfolio lost in a crash
questions.why: VaR = threshold loss at the confidence level (1−α) over the horizon; tail beyond is unspecified — the 'possible exceedance days' phrasing is the correct reading.
questions.trend: Known trap zone: ICAI objective papers repeatedly test limits/exceptions of this rule (pattern estimate).
questions.probWhy: Realistic likelihood for Nov 2026 — the probability-reading of VaR is the definition test AI prediction, not a certainty.

mem.tip: VaR names the line you cross on bad days; it never promises you won't cross it deeply.

questions.q: The key economic difference between hedging and speculation is:
o: Hedging reduces existing exposure; speculation creates exposure for profit
questions.why: Hedge = offset an exposure you already have; speculation = take an open position expecting to profit.
questions.trend: No dominant past-pattern signal; included for balanced coverage (AI judgement).
questions.probWhy: Lower likelihood but possible — the economic-intent distinction Included so a low-probability surprise cannot catch you cold.

mem.tip: Hedging buys certainty for a risk you have; speculation rents a risk you didn't.

questions.q: Scaling daily VaR to 10 days (i.i.d. returns) multiplies it by:
questions.why: Square-root-of-time rule with uncorrelated normal returns: 10-day ≈ daily × √10 — NOT ×10.
questions.trend: No dominant past-pattern signal; included for balanced coverage (AI judgement).

questions.q: Explain two agency conflicts in an Indian promoter-led company and how corporate governance mechanisms (board, regulation, market for corporate control) mitigate them; relate the answer to the wealth-maximisation objective.
questions.ans: Conflict 1: promoter vs minority — tunneling (related-party transactions, encashment of control benefits, preferative placements) extracting private benefits of control; mitigation: audit committee, minority-scheme rules (Reg 19/23 LODR — majority-of-minority approval for related-party schemes), independent directors, disclosure of RPTs. Conflict 2: shareholders vs managers — empire building, perquisite consumption, horizon mismatch (myopic quarterly vs long-term value); mitigation: incentive alignment (ESOPs, performance-linked pay with clawback), board monitoring, threat of takeover in the market for corporate control, debt discipline (free cash flow theory). Link to wealth maximisation: governance mechanisms re-anchor decisions to discounted cash-flow value rather than private benefits or accounting profits, protecting the residual claimants' valuation multiples.

questions.topic: Capital structure: trade-off vs pecking order
questions.q: Compare the static trade-off theory and the pecking order theory of capital structure. What does each predict about profitable versus unprofitable firms, and which fits Indian promoter-led firms better?
questions.ans: Trade-off: firms balance the tax shield of debt against expected distress/agency costs, implying a target D/E that is re-levered toward — profitable firms should carry MORE debt (bigger shields, lower distress risk). Pecking order (Myers–Majluf): asymmetric information makes internal funds first, debt second, equity last (equity issues are read as over-valuation, price drops) — implies profitable firms borrow LESS because they need less external finance. The two make opposite predictions for exactly the observable: high-profit firms' leverage. Indian context: high promoter control, costly rights issues, thin debt markets but abundant bank credit and collateral culture — pecking-order behaviour (promoter loans, IPO cash hoarding, reluctance to dilute) blends with trade-off discipline imposed by banks' covenant regimes. A full answer concludes that neither is 'true' — leverage policy is a target-with-grammar: a range governed by tax and distress, sequenced by information costs.

questions.q: Why do lenders impose covenants? Classify four covenant types with examples and explain the cost they impose on borrowers.
questions.ans: Covenants mitigate the shareholder–debtholder agency problem (asset substitution, dividend stripping, under-investment). Types: (i) negative pledge — no security to other lenders; (ii) leverage/coverage tests — max D/E, min interest cover, tested quarterly; (iii) distribution restrictions — cap dividends/buybacks until ratios met; (iv) investment restrictions — no capex/mergers beyond agreed limits without consent. Cost to borrower: lost flexibility — rejecting NPV-positive investments that trip a covenant (under-investment), higher effective cost via restricted actions, and 'technical default' renegotiation leverage to the lender (the covenant ratchet: a violation is a free option for the bank). Optimal covenants are tight enough to discipline, loose enough not to strangle — and they are cheaper than collateral for firms with good soft information, costlier for cyclicals (hence revolver-heavy structures).

questions.q: Equity Rs 2000 crore (required return 14%), debt Rs 1000 crore at 8% pre-tax, tax 25%. The CFO proposes a Rs 600 crore project with PV of inflows equal to 124% of cost. questions.ans: Weights: E/V = 66.7%, D/V = 33.3%; WACC = 14%×0.6667 + 8%×(0.75)×0.3333 = 11.33%. NPV = 1.24×600 − 600 = Rs 144.0 crore positive ⇒ accept. The 'because WACC is low' logic is WRONG: accept/reject compares project return to project RISK — WACC applies only if the project shares firm risk (same-line, same leverage); a riskier project must be discounted at a higher, relevered rate; the number here is a hurdle for this firm, not a verdict.

questions.q: Equity Rs 2000 crore (required return 14%), debt Rs 1000 crore at 8% pre-tax, tax 25%. The CFO proposes a Rs 400 crore project with PV of inflows equal to 124% of cost. Compute WACC, the project NPV at that discount, and state whether 'we should accept because WACC is low' is correct logic.
questions.ans: Weights: E/V = 66.7%, D/V = 33.3%; WACC = 14%×0.6667 + 8%×(0.75)×0.3333 = 11.33%. NPV = 1.24×400 − 400 = Rs 96.0 crore positive ⇒ accept. The 'because WACC is low' logic is WRONG: accept/reject compares project return to project RISK — WACC applies only if the project shares firm risk (same-line, same leverage); a riskier project must be discounted at a higher, relevered rate; the number here is a hurdle for this firm, not a verdict.

questions.q: Distinguish risk appetite, tolerance and capacity under ISO-31000/enterprise risk management, and describe the ERM process cycle with an example each for a listed manufacturer.
questions.ans: Capacity = the maximum risk the firm can absorb (capital, covenant, survival bounds — set by resources); Appetite = the amount and type of risk it WANTS to take in pursuit of strategy (board statement); Tolerance = entity-level/operational boundaries near the appetite (e.g., FX VaR ≤ 1.5% of net worth per desk). ERM cycle: (1) establish context (objectives, risk criteria); (2) identification — hazards, exposures (supply disruption, commodity); (3) analysis — likelihood × consequence, modeling (VaR, scenario); (4) evaluation — compare against appetite; (5) treatment — avoid/reduce/share/accept (hedging, insurance, redundancy); (6) monitor & review — KRIs, stress tests; plus communication across. Example: manufacturer accepts ≤25% unhedged oil exposure (tolerance), treats via collars; board reviews via monthly risk dashboard.
questions.scheme: Three definitions correctly differentiated — 4; process steps named with purpose — 4; worked mini-example per stage — 2.

questions.q: Distinguish total risk from systematic and unsystematic risk with the variance decomposition formula. What does diversification actually remove, and why can a well-diversified investor still lose money in a crash?
questions.ans: Total variance = systematic + idiosyncratic: σ²ᵢ = βᵢ²σ²ₘ + σ²εᵢ. Systematic (market) risk is common-factor movement no diversification removes — in an Indian crash the market factor is the whole loss driver; idiosyncratic risk (firm/industry-specific) averages toward zero with roughly 20–30 equally weighted stocks. A diversified investor still loses in a crash because the market factor itself fell: diversification guarantees the AVERAGE stock's performance, not protection from it. Further nuance: correlations rise in crises (contagion), so even the diversification benefit is state-dependent; and 'unsystematic' risks that are common within a sector (e.g., a power-tariff order) behave like systematic for sector-concentrated portfolios. Exam framing: beta prices systematic risk because markets cannot diversify it away; portfolios price nothing for risk any member could have shed alone.
questions.scheme: Decomposition equation — 2; what diversification removes/keeps — 2; crash & correlation-rise nuance — 2; pricing implication — 2.

questions.q: Distinguish the capital market line from the security market line: axes, what they price, validity for efficient and inefficient portfolios, and how each is used in practice.
questions.ans: CML: expected return vs TOTAL risk (σ), only efficient portfolios lie on it (rf + [(E(rₘ)−rf)/σₘ]σ); slope = market price of total risk = Sharpe of the market; an individual (inefficient) plot sits BELOW it — its idiosyncratic σ is uncompensated. SML: expected return vs BETA, every security and portfolio should lie on it under CAPM equilibrium (rf + β(E(rₘ)−rf)); used to judge ALL assets, good or bad, since beta is the only risk priced; a mispriced asset deviates above/below (alpha). Practice: CML tells the allocation between rf and the efficient fund (how much to lever), SML tells selection (which securities are cheap); α against SML is the skill measure, deviation below CML is an efficiency diagnosis. A trick both share: both require market portfolio, not any index — real indices only approximate.
questions.scheme: Axes & equations — 2; who lies on each — 2; efficient vs any asset — 2; practical use (allocation vs selection) — 2.

questions.q: Explain four behavioural biases that distort security valuation or portfolio decisions, and for each name a market anomaly it helps explain.
questions.ans: (i) Overconfidence — excessive trading and under-diversification; explains high turnover and why men trade more than funds should; also 'better-than-average' driver of empire M&A bids. (ii) Anchoring/conservatism — clinging to purchase price or old earnings; explains slow reaction to news (post-earnings-announcement drift) and resistance to re-rating. (iii) Loss aversion & disposition effect — selling winners early, riding losers (prospect theory curvature); explains momentum reversal and volume patterns near round-number price anchors. (iv) Herding/narrative cascades — simultaneous chasing of stories; explains bubbles, sector crowding (IT/Nifty Midcap sprees), and correlated panic selling that raises crisis correlations. Mitigations examiners want: process (checklists, pre-commit rules), outside view (base rates), and forcing functions (reverse DCF, kill criteria). Caveat line: behavioural finance augments, not replaces, CAPM-style pricing — arbitrage limits (costs, short-selling bans, noise-trader risk) let mispricing persist.
questions.scheme: Four biases × (mechanism + anomaly) — 6; mitigation — 1; limits-of-arbitrage caveat — 1.

questions.q: Compare scenario analysis, sensitivity analysis and Monte-Carlo simulation for a capital project; state what each adds beyond NPV and their key limitation.
questions.ans: Sensitivity: one variable at a time (% change to NPV; tornado ranking) — reveals drivers but ignores interactions and probabilities (each variable moved alone). Scenario: fixed coherent states (worst/base/best with joint shifts + probabilities → EMV and downside focus) — richer but arbitrary, few states captured. Simulation: distributions on inputs (demand, price, cost correlations), thousands of draws → NPV distribution — captures interaction, gives P(NPV<0) and percentiles; limitations: GIGO (garbage input), correlation assumptions, model risk. All three: risk-adjusted view vs single-point NPV at a risk-loaded discount rate; use alongside real-options logic (option to abandon/expand) for full picture.

questions.q: Project A: NPV Rs 60 crore, 4 years. Project B: NPV Rs 85 crore, 7 years. Both repeatable. Can NPV decide between them? Explain two remedies and when each breaks.
questions.ans: Raw NPV fails when lives differ because it ignores what happens after A's chain ends — the shorter project's cash flow can be reinvested into a repeat of itself. Remedy 1 — replacement chain (common-life): extend to LCM horizon (28 years, 7 A's vs 4 B's), rework the NPV over the common life; correct but ugly with discounting drift and needs true repeatability. Remedy 2 — equivalent annual annuity (EAA): EAA = NPV ÷ annuity factor at WACC; compare per-year value; algebraically identical to the chain under perfect repeatability. Both break when the decision is NOT repeatable: one-shot mine, capacity-limited concession (can't run two A's), or where future repeats face different prices/regulation — then neither chain nor EAA is right; instead use real-option framing or explicitly model the finite repeat horizon. Shortcut for exams: EAA of A = 60/AF(r,4), B = 85/AF(r,7) at given r; a positive EAA gap can flip against the NPV gap.

questions.q: Define real options and explain the option to WAIT, to ABANDON, and the option to EXPAND, each with one Indian-infrastructure example, noting why Black–Scholes inputs are hard here.
questions.ans: A real option is the right, not obligation, to change the project's cash-flow path when uncertainty resolves; NPV alone ignores that management ADAPTS. Option to wait (deferral): investing now kills the chance to invest at better information — a concession with pricing freedom or ROFR land is an American call on the project; value = NPV + waiting value, so a marginally-positive NPV can still mean 'not yet'. Example: a port terminal awaiting cargo-demand visibility; investing in year 0 forfeits the information value of a year of delay. Option to abandon: after year-3, if demand is low, sell the asset/redeploy the land — a put on liquidation value floor (resaleable plant; contractually returnable assets); it RAISES the project's minimum payoff and can flip a negative static NPV positive. Option to expand: first phase sized small, expansion rights (paid permit, spare land parcel, modular capacity) — a call on the growth NPV; phased capex is the cost of keeping the call alive. BS mapping pain: no traded asset = underlying (use DCF value of PV of inflows), exercise price = capex, variance must be proxied by price/volume history, and 'dividend' (cash flows lost by waiting) is the leak that shrinks the wait value.

questions.q: A firm has more positive-NPV projects than funds, and management distrusts the forecast numbers. Explain hard vs soft rationing, the profitability-index method and its flaw, and how a post-audit feeds the process.
questions.ans: Hard rationing: external funds truly unavailable (market for the firm's debt closed, covenants at the wall, information costs block a raise) — the cost of capital itself is not a market-clearing rate, so ranking under the budget constraint is unavoidable. Soft rationing: internal limits (management fear of over-commitment, decentralised risk ceilings) — theoretically the firm should relax and take all +NPV; its persistence is itself an agency signal. Ranking tool: profitability index PI = PV of inflows ÷ initial cost, highest-first until budget spent; flaw — PI is correct only for single-period capital limits and indivisible projects; it ignores scale and multi-period budgets (needs LP/IP programming: maximise ΣNPV s.t. period-wise outlay caps); a big project with lower PI can beat two small ones. Post-audit: compare realised vs forecast, compute NPV error decomposition (industry vs firm vs execution), no-blame culture for honest forecasts, penalise SANDBAGGING and promotion-optimism bias; feeds back as (i) adjusted risk premia per division and (ii) forecast-quality scorecards — this closes the loop making capital budgeting a learning system.

questions.q: Describe the three Fama efficiency forms with the test type that would falsify each.
questions.ans: Weak (past prices/technical rules give nothing): falsified by profitable chartist strategies tested by autocorrelation, run tests on returns; semi-strong (public info absorbed): falsified by abnormal returns to public signals — event studies around earnings/stock-splits, dividend announcements; strong (all info incl private): falsified by insider/board trading outperformance, mutual-fund persistence. questions.q: Distinguish free cash flow to firm and to equity in construction and in discount rate. When would you value an Indian bank or a leveraged LBO target with which, and why?
questions.ans: FCFF = cash available to ALL capital providers: EBIT(1−t) + D&A − capex − ΔWC; discount at WACC to get ENTERPRISE value, then equity = EV − net debt (+ non-operating assets). FCFE = cash to shareholders only: FCFF − interest(1−t) + net borrowing; discount at cost of equity — direct equity value, no bridge needed. Choice rules: FCFF when leverage is unstable or changing (LBO, turnaround, capital-structure transitions) because WACC is steadier than levered ke, and because debt's explicit flows cancel within FCFF mechanics; FCFE when the firm is stuck at a target leverage and the analyst must handle the financing schedule (bank/financial firms: debt is operations, so FCFE is awkward — these are usually valued on dividends/EXTRA models or EV multiples on adjusted operating profit). For a bank: neither standard FCFF — deposits are operating liabilities and interest is revenue-line; exam-safe statement: value a bank on dividend-discount or excess-return (residual income) framing, and an LBO target on FCFF-at-WACC with explicit debt schedule checks — never force FCFE on a company whose net borrowing swings wildly.

questions.topic: EVA and MVA — the value-based chain
questions.q: Define economic value added and market value added. Explain the adjustment logic EVA applies to accounting profit, and why an EVA-linked incentive plan changes behaviour more than an EPS-linked one.
questions.ans: EVA = NOPAT − WACC × capital employed (or NOPE: net operating profit after tax less a charge on the total capital used). Adjustments to accounting profit exist because GAAP is conservative for tax, not economics: capitalise-and-amortise large brand/advertising spends, add back R&D, reverse LIFO reserves, de-consolidate operating leases into debt (rent capitalised), strip non-operating assets from the base, provision-based smoothing, and adjust for unrecorded financing of receivables via securitisation (the Indian securitised book belongs in capital employed — ECL too). MVA = market cap − equity capital = present value of expected future EVA (the bridge that keeps EVA honest — a stream of EVA must reconcile to what the market pays). Incentive design: EPS rewards P&L-accretive but value-destroying scale (a low-margin acquisition adds EPS if financed cheaply yet earns below WACC); EVA shrinks the payout when capital earns below its cost, pushing divestment, capex discipline, and receivables/inventory tightening — it prices BALANCE-SHEET laziness that EPS misses. Pitfall line: EVA is period-myopic for long-gestation projects unless spends are capitalised (the adjustments ARE the fix) and is vulnerable to accounting games if not independently audited.

questions.q: List and explain five mistakes that routinely make a DCF confidently wrong, and state a check for each.
questions.ans: (i) Terminal-value dominance: TV is often 60–80% of value; check = compute TV share, run g ± 1% sensitivity, cross-check exit multiple implied. (ii) Mixing nominal and real: WACC nominal but cash flows real (or inflation in flows but not in discount rate) — check the inflation basis of g and of the rate together. (iii) FCF double-counting: treating depreciation as an outflow (real error) or ignoring replacement capex (fake growth) — check terminal capex = D&A (steady state) or the growth-consistency equation g = ROIC × reinvestment rate. (iv) Financing leakage: deducting interest in FCF then also loading WACC (or including asset cost in outflow AND in WACC via debt service) — check flows are pre-financing, discount carries the cost. (v) Cycle-blind base year: forecasting off a peak or trough; check = normalise margins to mid-cycle, test against multi-year averages. Additions that earn marks: perpetuity g above GDP forever (impossible size problem), ignoring dilution/ESOP in per-share equity value, and net-debt mistakes — minority interest and quasi-debt (unpaid advances) belong in the EV-to-equity bridge.

questions.q: Discuss MM irrelevance with its assumptions and the three major counter-arguments (bird-in-hand, tax differential, client-effect).
questions.ans: MM (1961): with perfect capital markets, given investment policy, dividend payout doesn't affect value — investors can manufacture payouts via homemade dividends (selling shares); value is driven by earning power of assets. Assumptions: no taxes/transaction costs, symmetric info, fixed investment, rational. Counter-1 Bird-in-hand (Gordon/Lintner): investors discount dividends at lower risk than capital gains ⇒ payout raises value (k falls with certainty) — MM rebut: risk of firm, not its split, prices equity. Counter-2 Tax: dividends taxed higher for many investors ⇒ prefer retention/capital gains; India: dividends taxed in company hands (FIT) shifts the balance — differential matters for FPIs/retirees. Counter-3 Client effect: clientele clusters (income vs growth) — changing policy re-prices via demand shifts, not cash flows; also signalling (information asymmetry): cuts signal trouble.

questions.q: Explain when a buyback beats a dividend, the signalling problems each creates, and the effect on EPS and leverage. Add the Indian route (open-market vs tender) tax angle.
questions.ans: Buyback vs dividend: a buyback is flexible, one-off, and return-of-capital — shareholders choose participation (tender), taxing only sellers at capital-gains rates (with indexation at their level), whereas a dividend is forced on all, taxed as income in hands (in India dividend tax sits with the SHAREHOLDER; companies pay no DDT — say this plainly). Buybacks suit: excess-cash firms wanting per-share growth without promising forever (dividends are sticky — cutting them is punished); undervaluation defence (the firm buys at its own discount); EPS boost (fewer shares, and if funded by debt or idle low-yield cash, net income per share rises arithmetically); leverage rises because equity shrinks (D/E on market value increases — MM-I says value mix-neutral but risk-shifts to equity). Signalling problems: dividend increase = management's confidence in durable earnings (the classic signal); buyback signal is noisier — 'cash-rich' positive vs 'no ideas' negative vs 'price-support/takeover defence' cynical; a buyback during a price crash can look like an option payout to insiders ahead of bad news, so disclosure windows (SEBI PIT quiet periods) police it. Open-market buybacks (company trades gradually, price discovery preserved) vs tender offer (fixed premium, instant, pro-rata fairness) — the tax and market-impact differences are the exam contrast. Watch the dilution mirror: a buyback at price ABOVE intrinsic value destroys value for non-tendering holders even as EPS rises — EPS up ≠ shareholders up.

questions.q: A shareholder complains that the company's dividend of Rs 2 per share is too small. Using MM's dividend irrelevance, explain what she can do herself and what frictions make the company's payout still matter.
questions.ans: Under MM (no taxes, no floatation, symmetric information), total return = the firm's investment policy only; the dividend SCHEDULE is separable: she can create a 'homemade dividend' by selling shares (or buying if the payout is too big — reinvest) — Rs 2/share desired ⇒ sell a small slice of the holding equal to the shortfall, or reinvest the excess; the pie size and the share count change, her wealth does not. Irrelevance proof in two lines: with fixed investment, payout = FCFE, so dividend per share = per-share claim of the same cash flows; changing the split between dividend and price merely moves value across her two pockets. Frictions that RELEVATE payout — the answer's body: taxes (dividend vs capital-gains rates differ and change with holding period and residence — in India both largely 10/12.5%-class in hands, but small-saver STCG exemption bands matter), floatation/transaction costs (selling 0.5% of a holding has brokerage and spread), behavioural preference for forced discipline (clients who cannot sell because willpower fails — the 'house money' effect), signalling (the cut is punished beyond arithmetic, so smoothing is rational), and illiquidity/private holdings (no market = no homemade lever). Conclusion: irrelevance is the benchmark; payout policy matters exactly as much as the frictions do — which is why firms 'manage' dividends rather than set them by formula.

questions.topic: Rights issues, bonuses and stock splits
questions.q: Distinguish a rights issue, a bonus issue and a stock split by their effect on cash, share count, capital accounts and theoretical price. Give the cum-rights theoretical ex-price formula with a numeric, and state the value of the right.
questions.ans: Cash: only the rights issue raises NEW money (existing holders subscribe at a discount to market); bonus and split raise nothing. Share count: rights adds shares to SUBSCRIBING holders (non-subscribers are diluted — hence the renounceable variant lets them sell the right instead of losing value); bonus and split multiply every holding pro-rata, leaving ownership percentages unchanged. Capital accounts: bonus transfers free reserves/share premium INTO paid-up capital (ineligible reserves — revaluation surpluses, debit P&L balances — cannot be capitalised); a split only cuts face value (paid-up total untouched); rights increases paid-up at par with the premium above par going to share premium. Theoretical price: cum-rights 400, shares 10 crore, 1 rights share at 250 per 5 held (2 crore new) ⇒ TEP = (400x10 + 250x2)/12 = Rs 375; value of right = cum − TEP = Rs 25 per existing share — the renounceable right is this figure traded. Bonus numeric: 1 bonus per 5 at cum 420 ⇒ TEP = 420x5/6 = 350 — pure re-labelling, wealth-neutral; market reaction is all signal (confidence in cash generation vs the rights message: 'we need money, and here is the discount'). Splits: 10-face to 2-face at 500 ⇒ 100 post-split — retail-access engineering, zero wealth transfer. Examiners reward ending the comparison table with what each says about management intent.

questions.q: List CAPM's assumptions, and explain how Arbitrage Pricing Theory relaxes them — stating APT's equation structure.
questions.ans: CAPM: single-factor (market), homogeneous expectations, risk-free lending/borrowing at one rate, no taxes/transaction costs/frictions, infinitely divisible, all mean-variance optimisers ⇒ every asset on SML with E(R)=rf+β(Rm−rf). APT relaxes: investors need not all optimise identically, multiple systematic factors possible (inflation, industrial production, rates, oil) — returns R = a + ΣβiFi + e; no-arbitrage ⇒ expected returns linear in betas with factor premia λi; firm-specific risk diversified; equilibrium not required — mispricings arbitraged. Practical: multi-factor models (Fama-French: size, value + market) — use for cost-of-capital estimation where pure CAPM betas unstable.

questions.q: Explain how attribution analysis decomposes a portfolio's excess return over its benchmark, naming each component and its sign convention, and why sector allocation can look 'lucky' while selection looks 'skilful'.
questions.ans: Brinson–Hood–Beebower splits excess return Rₚ − R_b into (i) ALLOCATION: Σ (wₚᵢ − w_bᵢ)×(R_bᵢ − R_b) — did the manager overweight the sectors that beat the market? (ii) SELECTION: Σ wₚᵢ×(Rₚᵢ − R_bᵢ) — within the sectors held, did the names beat their sector? (iii) INTERACTION: Σ (wₚᵢ − w_bᵢ)(Rₚᵢ − R_bᵢ) — the cross term (allocation AND selection right together); pure-formula variants (BF) fold interaction into selection. Signs: overweighting a lagging sector makes allocation negative whatever the stock-picking did. Why allocation looks luck: sector moves (banking rally, IT derating) are macro/regulatory events the manager does not control; a single-year +200 bps from riding Nifty IT is a coin-toss skill story — attribution must be tested across periods and against an allocation model (information ratio, t-stat) before calling it a style. Selection looks like skill because within a sector the manager chose — but selection in a concentrated book is also the sector bet relabelled (only 3 private banks = 'selection' vs a 40-stock spread). Practice for exams: state the three parts, give a two-sector numeric, and close with 'attribution explains, it does not prove skill — significance lives in time-series of components'.

questions.q: Define portfolio drift and rebalancing. Explain the no-trade band policy versus calendar rebalancing, list three costs of rebalancing, and state how an investor's age and taxes should shift the policy.
questions.ans: Drift: assets grow at different rates, so weights wander — a 60/40 equity-debt mix in a bull market becomes 72/28 within a year, silently re-risking the plan. Rebalancing restores target weights. Method 1 — calendar: fixed dates; simple, disciplined, but may rebalance at bad moments and ignores how far drift went. Method 2 — bands: trade only when a weight breaches ±X (absolute or relative); fewer trades in calm markets, acts when it matters, but needs monitoring and can chase in trending markets (buy-back-the-crash risk). Rebalancing is contrarian by construction: you sell rallies, buy falls — behaviourally hard and statistically modest in expected-return terms (it harvests mean-reversion of assets' relative returns, and if markets are trend-driven it can hurt: 'rebalancing is insurance, not alpha'). Costs: transaction costs/brokerage & spread; taxes (selling appreciated equity above the STCG/LTCG thresholds crystallises liability — Indian equity LTCG > 1.25 lakh taxed, debt gains taxed in slab: asset-location in taxable accounts); and information/decision friction. Age & tax shifts: younger can tolerate wider bands and let equity drift (more time to re-risk); pre-retiree tighter bands (sequence risk dominates); in a tax-sheltered account (EPF/PPF-like) band-rebalance freely, in taxable accounts prefer NEW-MONEY rebalancing — direct inflows to the underweight side, selling only when a band is grossly breached. That is the marks-earning structure.

questions.q: Compare VaR and expected shortfall; then explain what stress testing adds that both models cannot, and why the 2008 crisis made stress testing mandatory in risk frameworks.
questions.ans: VaR_q = the loss not exceeded with probability q over a horizon, from the q-quantile of the P&L distribution (e.g. 1-day 99% VaR Rs 12 Cr ⇒ on average one day in 100 loses more than 12; nothing about how much more). Methods: variance–covariance (fast, breaks under fat tails), historical (real tails, no extrapolation, window-dependent), Monte Carlo (model everything, model-fragile). VaR's flaws: no convexity above the quantile (tail-blind), not sub-additive in general (can penalise diversification), and pro-cyclical (calm regimes shrink VaR, leverage grows just as risk builds). Expected shortfall (CVaR): mean loss GIVEN beyond VaR — coherent, tail-sensitive, the Basel replacement for traded-risk. Stress testing answers the question VaR cannot: 'what if the model itself and the regime are wrong' — historical replays (2008, 2013 taper tantrum for INR), hypothetical shocks (rates +300 bps, INR −10%), and reverse stress tests (what breaks us, then how likely is it). 2008 lesson: VaR systems saw 'within model' losses daily while correlation breakdowns made the portfolio's actual tail lethal; models estimated tails from quiet samples (the 'calm was the sample' problem), so regulators (Basel, RBI ICAAP) forced stress + reverse-stress into capital planning — stress tests now set capital floors, VaR sets limits.

questions.q: A client demands 9.5% expected return; rf 6%, index fund (market) 13%, σm 20%. Using only the risk-free asset and the index fund, find the allocation, the portfolio's expected return check and its σ — and say what the client's demand fixes exactly (risk or return).

The target return fixes RISK (the client must accept 10% σ on the CML) — or they must accept a point BELOW the CML (a worse fund/manager); no free lunch on return vs risk when markets are efficient.

questions.q: Explain four motives for securitizing receivables and two costs/risks it creates for the originator. Distinguish the structure from factoring.
questions.ans: Motives: (i) funding-cost arbitrage — a pool of high-rated consumer/loan receivables can borrow cheaper (AAA senior tranche at near-AA rates) than the originator's own balance sheet (bankruptcy-remote, over-collateralised), so cost of funds falls even with servicing fees paid; (ii) asset–liability duration match — fund long receivables with matching-dated pools instead of short deposits/CP, killing a rollover risk the originator cannot hedge; (iii) capital & ratio management — a true sale removes risk-weighted assets (capital relief for NBFCs/banks; if the structure keeps first-loss, rating agencies still charge capital — exam nuance: 'relief only to the extent of risk truly transferred'); (iv) origination-scale economics — earning on fees and on the spread between asset yield and the securitised funding rather than on the float, so the balance sheet turns over faster (the 'originate-to-distribute' model). Costs/risks: retained first-loss and reputational support (implicit recourse — the 2008 lesson: sponsors rescued doomed vehicles to protect their franchise, so 'transferred risk' came home), plus covenant/liquidity mismatch (trust needs timely collections; servicing failures trigger spread widening), and disclosure/consolidation accounting (retained interests fair-valued; SPE consolidation when control economics persist). Factoring vs securitization: factoring = sale (often recourse) of SHORT-term trade receivables with collection/credit protection as a SERVICE, priced per invoice; securitization = term transaction building marketable DEBT from a diversified pool, priced on tranche credit, no vendor-management service. One line: factoring finances invoices; securitization finances an asset book — via the capital markets.

questions.q: Classify internal versus external credit enhancement and explain, with a structure of your choice, the order in which the first rupee of loss falls.
questions.ans: Internal (built into the pool structure, paid by investors' subordinate cash): (i) SUBORDINATION/tranches — equity/C and mezzanine B absorb losses first, protecting senior A; (ii) OVERCOLLATERALISATION — Rs 110 of assets per Rs 100 of rated notes; (iii) RESERVE (cash collateral) ACCOUNT — months of collections parked, usually the front-most layer; (iv) EXCESS SPREAD — asset yield minus note coupon + fees routed to a notional account before being released to the residual holder (the annual repair fund that catches inflow-year losses before touching principal layers). External (third-party promises): monoline insurance/guarantees (rare in India, common abroad), letters of credit, corporate guarantees from a creditworthy parent (only as good as the guarantor — correlated failure is the catch: parent distress often coincides with pool distress), and cash-collateral swaps. Loss waterfall (e.g. senior 85, mezz 10, equity 5, reserve 4, excess spread 2%/yr): a default loss runs (1) excess spread for the year, (2) reserve, (3) equity C, (4) mezz B, (5) then and only then senior A — enhancement thickness per tranche = what the rating must survive. The exam trap: external wraps move risk, they do not erase correlation; internal layers move risk into the capital structure's own body.

questions.q: Explain a mortgage pass-through and the negative convexity it creates. Define PSA-style prepayment speed intuition (no formula), and how pooling structure (serial vs fully amortising vs IO/PO strips) addresses it.
questions.ans: A pass-through pools mortgages, collects their monthly payments net of servicing, and passes principal+interest pro-rata to investors. The homeowner's option breaks the investor's math: when rates fall, borrowers refinance — principal returns EARLY, at par, exactly when reinvestment rates are low: the 'shortening duration' side of negative convexity (price rises stop at par; falls accelerate when spreads blow out). When rates rise, prepayments freeze, duration extends into pain — convexity goes the wrong way in both tails: 'the borrower holds a free call on your yield'. Prepayment speed is quoted as an annualised fraction of the remaining balance (CPR) with vintage patterns (slow, ramping, decaying — PSA framing); what matters to value is the path, not the point estimate. Structures: SERIAL pools self-hedge (short maturities mix in); level-payment fully-amortising pools spread the option; and the classic surgical answer — STRIPS: interest-only (IO) strips (cash flow rises when prepayments rise — a natural long-convexity hedge) and principal-only (PO) strips (buy at discount, gain when prepayments accelerate — the investor's mirrored bet). An issuer may issue IO to investors who want the prepayment exposure. Conclusion for exams: pass-through risk is an EMBEDDED SHORT CALL sold to homeowners; structuring and stripping redistribute it but never destroy it.

questions.q: Why did SEBI impose a fixed scheme-category framework for mutual funds? Explain its mechanics (core categories, label discipline) and how it protects the retail investor while creating new problems.
questions.ans: The problem: before 2017 funds multiplied with overlapping, re-labelled portfolios — a 'balance plan' here, a 'multi-cap there', the same fund sliding into whatever theme won (style drift), investors comparing apples to renamed oranges, and a daisy-chain of relaunches to reset expense caps or chase hot flows. The framework: fixed core categories for each type (equity: large cap, mid cap, multi cap, ELSS, focused, sectoral/thematic…; debt: overnight, liquid, gilt, corporate bond, credit risk, target maturity…; hybrid: conservative-aggressive, balanced-advantage, multi-asset…) with mandated minimum exposure rules (e.g. large-cap: 80% in top-100 by market cap; credit-risk: 65% in below-AA), ONE fund per category per AMC (no duplication), and the AMFI/TMU unified codes; labels must match the portfolio in substance, changes need notice, exit loads and TER are capped. Protection: like-for-like comparison, category benchmarks for evaluation, no surprise risk migration, predictable liquidity tiers for debt. New problems: categories become CLOSETS — the top-100 cap on large-caps forces mechanical buying regardless of price (index-in-a-box for active money); a fund can be trapped holding bad mid-caps to keep its exposure while the fund manager 'manages around the box'; thematic proliferation returned (every thematic must fit a category — so 'energy' became 'sectoral' — and AMC churn into whichever theme is allowed and hot); and the ONE-fund rule pushes consolidation into larger existing funds mid-holding, creating tax-inefficiency and forced flows. Exam conclusion: categorisation trades style-drift risk for box constraint — a net win for retail comparison, a cost to active flexibility.

questions.q: A client asks: why do most active funds underperform their index over 10 years, yet charging 2% is defensible? Answer with the zero-sum-with-costs argument and name the situations where active management should have an edge.
questions.ans: The arithmetic (Sharpe's subtraction method): gross active returns of all investors net to ~zero before cost (the market IS the aggregate of them); after cost, the average active fund must underperform the index BY total costs — a 1.8% average fee means the average holder loses ~1.8% to the index before any skill, and most Indian large-cap actives have underdone the Nifty 50 TRI over long windows exactly by their TER. Fees are defensible ONLY where the game is not efficient enough for the subtraction argument to bind: (i) small/micro caps — few analysts, low float, illiquidity premium the patient active can harvest; (ii) credit — private negotiation, covenant work, default recovery: alpha lives in the debt desk; (iii) event/thematic dislocations (demergers, stake sales, fraud detection — the active that exits the Satyam early earns its fee forever); (iv) tax and flow management for the client (loss harvesting, holding-period arbitrage) which the index doesn't offer; (v) mandates with liability constraints (insurance ALM, EPF-like glidepaths) where benchmark-matching is not the objective. Practical verdict wording: 'for the large-cap core, index; for the inefficient edges, active with capacity limits — and pay active only where its sources are visible'. Capacity and fee honesty: alpha decays with AUM (small-cap active at 5,000 Cr is a mid-cap fund in disguise); and a fund that outperforms after a fee of 0.4% is the fee you actually keep.
questions.scheme: Zero-sum-with-costs — 3; evidence sentence (India long-window) — 1; four/five inefficiency sources — 3; capacity & verdict — 1.
keyPoints: Small caps, credit, events, taxes, liability mandates

questions.q: Explain how a mutual fund's NAV is computed and how dividends, entry/exit flows and valuation practices distort the return an investor perceives. Give the arithmetic of a dividend adjustment.
questions.ans: NAV = (assets − liabilities)/units: portfolio marked to exchange quotes (equity: closing price; illiquid debt: indicative yields from a valuation committee/AMFI-style matrix, not trade price — the mark is a policy, not a fact), accrued income added, expenses (TER deducted daily from corpus, not charged to the investor separately), flows: money in after 15:30 (T) invests at T+1 NAVs; large-redemption anti-dilution via exit load or in-kind redemption (protects stayers — a point of trust). Distortion 1 — dividend: NAV drops exactly by the distribution (cum NAV 45.20, div 2.00 ⇒ ex 43.20); a 'yield' of 4.4% with a flat year is returning your own rupee — the return that year was zero; ex-div total return = (43.20 + 2.00)/45.20 − 1 = 0.0%; the 'dividend option looks safer than growth option' fallacy rests here (post-2018, dividends are taxed in hands at slab rates, so the growth option's tax deferral is the actual difference). Distortion 2 — flow timing: a redemption paid from cash held for T+1 settlement dilutes the stayers on inflow day and forces forced sales on outflow day; large inflows in a rally buy NAVs the market will mark down (and vice versa) — hence the 'cash drag' tax on all. Distortion 3 — debt marks: matrix yields lag a spread blowout by days (a fund can hold a bond at 100 the market would clear at 92 — the NAV is 'the last time we checked'). Exam use of all this: judge a fund on TRI and rolling-window relative numbers, never point NAVs or dividend yield.
questions.scheme: NAV construction — 2; dividend arithmetic — 2; flow dilution — 1; debt-mark lag — 1; TRI verdict — 1.
keyPoints: Div cuts NAV by face of gift

questions.q: Compare option-based and futures-based hedging for an equity portfolio manager who fears a market fall but wants to stay invested (long horizon, tax-sensitive to sales).
questions.ans: Futures hedge: short index futures (β-adjusted contracts N = V×β/f×Index) — symmetric: removes downside AND upside; daily margin/cash-flow management; no premium cost; basis risk. Options hedge: put protection (protective puts) or collar (sell OTM call to fund OTM put) — keeps upside (put) at a premium, or band-limits both (collar) near-zero cost; no margin outflow for buyers, path-dependent; Greeks change hedge ratio; time decay vs futures carry. Decision factors: cost of premium (implied vol), confidence in view, tax (futures gains frequent/short-term; option premium losses timing), liquidity in index options; tail-risk protection favours options when the fall is unlikely-but-painful.

questions.q: Define delta, gamma, theta and vega. Explain, for a dealer long a large call, what each says about tomorrow's P&L and why gamma and theta are the same trade in two currencies.
questions.ans: Delta = ∂V/∂S (how much option value moves with a one-unit underlying move): long 0.6-call ⇒ +0.6 per rupee up, hedge by shorting 0.6 shares per contract (the hedge ratio lives here). Gamma = ∂²V/∂S² = ∂Δ/∂S: the curvature — ATM long options have peak gamma; when S moves, delta re-hedges itself in the RIGHT direction for a long option (buy the dip, sell the rally), which is why long-gamma positions can profit from pure movement (day-trade P&L of delta-hedged position ≈ ½Γ(ΔS)²). Theta = time decay per day (value bleeding as the option approaches expiry), largest ATM. Vega = per 1% volatility: long options are long uncertainty. The dealer long the call: tomorrow = Δ×move + ½Γ×move² − Θ×day + ν×(ΔIV). The key structural line: gamma and theta are the SAME trade priced in two currencies — a delta-hedged long-gamma position pays time-decay RENT for the right to rebalance on moves (long Γ = long optionality = short time; short Γ = harvest theta but own the tail risk); no free gamma in equilibrium (the tension is the Black–Scholes pricing itself). Convexity shrinks near expiry (Γ explodes as ATM decay accelerates — the pin risk zone), and vega and gamma both concentrate in the ATM band — which is why vol traders care about the term structure.
questions.scheme: Four definitions with formulas — 3; P&L decomposition for the dealer — 2; gamma–theta one-trade insight — 2; expiry/pin nuance — 1.
keyPoints: Γ = re-hedges in your favour when long
Γ–Θ two currencies of one trade

questions.q: State put-call parity for European options and explain its three uses: arbitrage (conversion/reversal), pricing the third leg from the two traded, and creating synthetic positions. Why does American-style early exercise weaken the equality?
questions.ans: Parity: C + Ke^(−rT) = P + S₀ (same strike/expiry, on a non-dividend underlying; with dividends the PV of dividends drops S). Proof intuition: a call plus a cash-parked strike replicates a put plus the stock — both sides pay max(S, K): hold either box, end identically, so pay the same or arbitrage. Uses: (1) arbitrage — if left side < right, buy the underpriced call+bond, sell the overpriced put+stock (conversion; reversal for the other mispricing) — the profit is riskless because expiry payoffs cancel exactly; index arbitrage in Indian F&O is this same logic with future replaces the bond (C − P ≈ F − K discounted); (2) pricing — when one leg is missing or mispriced (deep ITM options where bid-asks are wide), compute it from the other two — this is what exchanges and brokers actually do for illiquid strikes; (3) synthetics — long stock = long call + short put (protective collar flipped), protective put = long call + long put... every 'position from parts' table is parity read sideways (this is how a hedge without cash is built: the synthetic long via options around a locked-in capital budget). American options: parity becomes an INEQUALITY because early exercise has value only on the deep-ITM American put (interest on K) and deep-ITM calls on non-dividend stocks (never early — say so, then caveat with dividends); the holder's timing option can't be replicated by the static European side, so bounds: C − P ≤ S − PV(K) etc., only a no-arbitrage RANGE survives — widened by the early-exercise value and concentrated in deep-ITM puts when rates are high. Safe framing: parity holds exactly for European exercise; American options give bounds, not equality.

questions.q: Explain index arbitrage between the futures and the cash market, its limits in India, and how it enforces cost-of-carry pricing.
questions.ans: Mechanics: when F > S(1+(r−q)t) (futures rich to fair value), buy the basket (or ETF) and sell futures — the basis locks a riskless gain converging to zero at expiry (sell cash, unwind short); when cheap, reverse: short the basket where borrow exists, buy futures. In India the practical long side uses an ETF basket or Nifty 50 replication (few funds permit simultaneous short baskets of 50 names; stock-borrow (SLB) is shallow, costly and recallable — the reverse arbitrage is structurally weaker than the forward one). Limits: transaction costs (market-impact of 50-order legs, ETF premium/discount to NAV), borrow unavailability and rebate fees, T+1 settlement mismatch (a one-day leg risk that eats thin arb margins — the cash-future legs don't close simultaneously), execution-latency races (arbitrageurs compete down the basis to the cost floor), and the 'squeezed leg' tail (recall of borrowed stock mid-spread converts arb to direction). Enforcement story: because the forward arm is cheap and mechanical (buy basket, short futures, hold), the futures float barely above carry; the discount arm stays wider than premium — the asymmetry itself is a favourite exam observation. Note the expiry-day twist: Indian Nifty futures settle on last-Thursday cash values, so convergence is administratively enforced too — an arb that assumes perfect convergence ignores the 3:00–3:30 quote window risk that has burned desks (that window = the 'expiry pin' risk line).
questions.scheme: Both arms — 2; Indian constraints (SLB, T+1, impact) — 2; why the discount arm underworks — 1; expiry-convergence nuance — 1.

questions.topic: Black-Scholes inputs and their Indian proxies
questions.q: List the five Black-Scholes inputs, say which are directly observable for an NSE-listed stock option, and explain how each unobservable input is estimated and how errors in them distort a hedge or an ESOP charge.
questions.ans: Inputs: (1) spot S — traded, exact (closing price; mind ex-div dates); (2) strike K — contractual, exact; (3) time to expiry T — exact, but convert trading-day expiry conventions to calendar time correctly; (4) risk-free rate r — use the sovereign yield at matching tenor (91-day T-bill for short-dated NSE options, interpolated G-sec for long tenors) — not call money or FD rates; (5) volatility sigma — the only genuinely unobservable input: historical sigma (e.g. EWMA on daily returns) as the prior, and implied vol from traded options as a market-consensus readout. The circularity trap: pricing an option with the implied vol from that same option reveals the market quote, not an independent value — implied vol is for comparing and hedging, not for valuation. Distortions: sigma error hits vega proportionally (an ATM 1-month option moves several percent of spot for a 10% relative vol error — enough to flip an Ind AS 102 ESOP charge); ignoring discrete dividends overprices calls and over-hedges; using a deposit rate instead of the sovereign rate misstates thin long-dated values. Framing line: BS assumes constant vol, lognormal prices and frictionless markets — all violated in gap-prone NSE conditions, so treat BS as a quoting convention, not truth.
questions.scheme: Five inputs with observability — 2; proxy sources (G-sec, EWMA/implied) — 3; dividend treatment — 1; error-direction analysis — 2; assumption caveat — 1.

questions.q: A mid-size auto-components exporter faces transaction, translation and economic exposure. Design a risk-management programme: policy, instruments and measurement — state why hedging economic exposure is different in nature.
questions.ans: Policy layer: board-approved exposure limits (gross/net by tenor — e.g., 100% of 3-month confirmed receivables, 50% of 6–12), functional currency analysis (Ind AS 21), hedge-accounting choice (Ind AS 109 CF hedge with effectiveness testing). Instruments: forwards for locked flows; options for unconfirmed/tender-linked (buy-out when awarded); natural hedges (currency invoicing match, local sourcing, lead-lag on flexible flows). Translation: balance-sheet net exposure minimised by funding-in-currency rule (debt aligns with sub's currency); OCI volatility disclosed. Economic: long-run competitiveness shift (a stronger INR erodes margins regardless of hedges) — cannot be hedged with derivatives; treated by operating strategy (pricing power, product mix, cost base shift, market diversification). Measurement: VaR on residual open, hedge-effectiveness stats, exposure reports monthly with sensitivity tables; audit trail; no-speculation mandate.

questions.q: Define economic exposure and distinguish it from transaction and translation exposure. Show how a rupee appreciation changes a software exporter's value through channels that never touch a single contract, and list the strategic (non-financial) hedges.
questions.ans: Transaction exposure: contractual rupee value of already-priced flows — measurable, hedgeable with forwards (the mechanical one). Translation: accounting-only remeasurement of foreign books on consolidation (OCI volatility, no cash flow) — structural. Economic exposure = the change in firm VALUE from unexpected FX moves through the FUTURE cash-flow stream itself — competitor prices, demand elasticities, sourcing shifts and margin compression in an environment where competitors' home currencies move; it exists even with zero foreign contracts (a purely domestic cement maker faces peso-cheap imported clinker). Software exporter with +10% INR: (1) billings are dollar contracts but their RUPEE value falls one-for-one; (2) pricing is competitive — raise INR prices and lose deals to global peers, so rates stay flat while INR wage costs (the real cost base, priced in rupees!) FALL — the margin cushion absorbs; the value change = a mix of pass-through, wage-elasticity and deal-flow shifts — and a strong rupee over 2–3 years compresses wage-inflation-adjusted talent costs, restoring margin; (3) demand destruction if clients defer projects; (4) wage arbitrage erosion vs Vietnam/Poland. Non-financial hedges (the marks): production/site location matching (build the centre in the currency you earn — 'natural hedge'), sourcing in the revenue currency, market diversification (revenue in many currencies = portfolio variance reduction), pricing-currency re-negotiation (index clauses, INR billing to domestic customers), capacity flexibility (idle plant switchable across geos), and financial hedging only of the CONTRACTED tail. The exam one-liner: economic exposure is where value comes from cash-flow expectations; hedges that move the BUSINESS beat hedges that move the P&L statement.

questions.q: A company has issued a USD 150m bond while earning rupees. Explain the currency-swap conversion mechanics and risks; then why 'cheap foreign debt' can be the most expensive debt a company owns.
questions.ans: Mechanics: the swap converts the USD cash-flow profile into INR without touching the bond: at inception exchange notional (INR received at spot against USD delivered to... in a loan hedge typically: borrower receives USD each period from the swap counterparty, pays INR fixed — the USD leg services the coupon and redemption; the INR leg is the company's actual outlay). Net result: a rupee-denominated cost of debt = USD coupon + swap spread − INR-USD interest-rate-differential benefit — the swap prices the forward curve implicitly: since INR rates exceed USD rates by roughly the forward premium, converting a LOW-coupon USD loan to INR often nets out to a rupee cost at or above the domestic market rate: the 'cheap' 5% USD debt becomes a 9.2% INR equivalent when the cross-currency basis is priced (the carry was never free — the rupee must DEPRECIATE ~4.2%/yr just to break even unhedged; that is the forward math talking). Risks: (i) counterparty (swap provider default at INR shortage — the 2008 lesson) mitigated by ISDA/CSA collateral and, for corporates, bank-led structures; (ii) basis risk — USD funding rates (SOFR-linked) vs bond coupon, and the NDF/ondshore INR rate mismatch; (iii) notional mismatch as debt amortises (swaps must mirror schedule, or run a bullet and roll); (iv) collateral/margin on the derivative if not collateral-friendly (liquidity call); (v) accounting — fair-value volatility if hedge designation fails (cash-flow hedge accounting needed, Ind AS 109 effectiveness testing). The 'why expensive' close: unhedged FX debt borrows the future rupee at a forward discount, converting each depreciation into principal growth — the ECA stats (many Indian infra cos 2013: USD loans with INR at 40→68 = +70% principal without one new loan) — the classic lesson: foreign debt is cheap only until it is catastrophic; its coupon is a deductible on a claim you cannot size.

questions.q: A country devalues; its trade balance worsens before improving. Draw the logic (Marshall–Lerner, contracts, pricing-to-market) and say what decides how long the downturn leg lasts.
questions.ans: Two legs: right after devaluation, QUANTITIES are contractual and sticky — exports were priced in foreign currency (revenue per unit in local terms unchanged… careful: export receipts in INR rise, import payments in INR rise) — the DOMINANT effect is VALUE: the same quantities now cost more in rupees (imports) while export volumes can't surge until new orders form — the trade balance (in value terms) deteriorates if import demand is price-insensitive, until volumes re-optimise. The condition that decides direction over time is Marshall–Lerner: net improvement requires Σ(ηₓ+ηₘ) > 1 (long-run elasticities exceed short-run — contracts, certification, sourcing, buyer-switching costs keep short-run elasticities small — that is the 'J' dip). Pricing-to-market: exporters with margin compression (absorb, keep the foreign price) deliberately delay pass-through and reprice later (so export volumes improve before prices — extending the dip); importers in India often pass through fully, shrinking demand fast. Duration of the downward leg: contract tenor and pricing-currency mix (share billed in own currency), lead-lag in invoicing (the same exposure the corporate treasurer hedges for 90 days), supply capacity (can exporters actually ramp?), and confidence effects (if devaluation reads as policy failure, capital flight offsets the trade gain — twin crises). For a CORPORATE on P2 terms: a devaluation's export windfall is an operating call struck at today's volumes; its import-bill cost is certain — the asymmetry IS the J for firms too.

questions.q: State and briefly derive the intuition for IRP (covered), PPP (relative), FIS and the international Fisher relation; note what each implies for a treasurer choosing between domestic and foreign borrowing.
questions.ans: Covered IRP: F/S = (1+rh)/(1+rf) — the forward premium/discount equals interest differential; no arbitrage ⇒ hedged foreign borrowing ≡ domestic (cost parity). PPP relative: %ΔS ≈ πh − πf ⇒ prices in common currency tend to equal. Fisher (each country): 1+i = (1+r)(1+π) ⇒ real rates equalise across open economies. International Fisher: %ΔS ≈ iH − iF — currencies with higher nominal rates depreciate by the differential. Treasurer's takeaway: after FORWARD hedge, borrowing cost advantage in cheaper-rate currency vanishes; unhedged foreign-currency debt is a view on PPP/UIRP failing in the short run (real-world deviations: capital controls, risk premia, sticky prices — the 2010s carry trades). So choice must weigh deviation risk vs rate saving.
questions.scheme: Each of four relations: statement + one-line derivation/intuition — 6 (1.5 each); treasurer's implication (hedged parity, view on deviation) — 3; short-run deviations examples — 1.

questions.topic: Duration and convexity in bond management
questions.q: Define Macaulay, modified and effective duration and convexity. A 10-year bond (8%, semi-annual) trades at par. Approximate its price change for +150 bps using duration with convexity adjustment and say why the correction goes both ways.
questions.ans: Macaulay duration = weighted average time of cash flows (years); modified = Mac/(1+y/m) — price sensitivity per unit yield change; EFFECTIVE duration is measured for bonds with embedded options (price to a parallel shift of the whole curve, not yield-only), and convexity = the second derivative of price-yield (the curvature). Arithmetic (8%, semi, 10y): MacDur ≈ 7.24, ModDur ≈ 6.95; ΔP/P ≈ −D*×Δy + ½C×Δy². With Δy = 1.5%: duration gives −10.43%; the convexity correction (typical C ≈ 61 for this bond): +½×61×(0.015)² ≈ +0.68% ⇒ ≈ −9.75%. Why both ways: the price-yield curve is convex toward the origin — for a YIELD RISE the curve lies above the tangent line (loss smaller than linear says), for a YIELD FALL the same geometry adds to the gain (gain bigger than linear): the tangent under-predicts in both directions — that is what 'positive convexity pays in both tails' means; bonds with negative convexity (callable, mortgage pools) reverse the sign (price capped at call, falls exceed duration). Portfolio management use: (i) match duration to horizon (the zero-coupon = pure immunisation insight), (ii) when the curve shifts non-parallel, modified duration lies — key-rate and bullet/barbell ladders hedge the shape, not just the level, (iii) convexity itself is a scarce, priced good: high-convexity (low coupon, long maturity) portfolios outperform after big moves whichever way they come, and underperform in stable times (paid in spread).

keyPoints: Convexity beats tangent in BOTH tails

questions.q: A pension must pay Rs 400 crore exactly 8 years from now. Design an immunisation programme and explain its fragility: what breaks it even if the initial match is exact.
questions.ans: Immunisation = match portfolio duration to the liability horizon while minimising the spread of cash-flow times (Baranchuk–Redington): a single zero-coupon 8-year bond matched to PV is exact; a barbell or laddered mix with D = 8 and convexity > liability's protects against small parallel yield moves (duration match ⇒ first-order insensitivity; convexity higher ⇒ price above the tangent whichever way the curve moves). Construction: value the liability at the current curve, buy a portfolio of the same PV with Mac/Mod duration 8 (or 7.8 after compounding), keep cash flows' dispersion above the liability's (for a single date, any dispersion is 'excess' — but real portfolios want the minimum consistent with liquidity), and RE-BALANCE when time passes (duration decays at different rates on asset and liability legs). Fragility (the exam's meat): (1) PARALLEL assumption — a flattening with a steep short end (rates up at 2y, down at 30y) leaves the asset mix mis-priced vs the single 8-year point — key-rate durations (KRD per maturity bucket) hedge the SHAPES, and an 8-year liability has ~zero KRD elsewhere; a barbell at 3/15y mimics duration but fails at twist; (2) RE-INVESTMENT drift: if coupons of the barbell reinvest at changed rates, PV math shifts — the two offsetting effects (price vs reinvestment) only cancel exactly for a zero; (3) TIME: after a year the asset duration ≠ 7 and the liability ≠ 7 unless rebalanced — immunisation is a rolling discipline; (4) convexity shortfall after large parallel moves, and (5) credit: spread widening on corporate holdings is not a rate move — immunised only against rates, not spreads — so the liability-matching instrument class (G-sec) matters (India's EPFO largely does this: gilts to horizon).

keyPoints: Coupons re-invest, offset for zeros only

questions.q: Explain bullet, barbell and ladder portfolios and when each outperforms, plus the carry-rollover decomposition of return and the 'riding the yield curve' trade.
questions.ans: Three shapes against the same duration target: BULLET — one maturity (pure rate play, high convexity vs the ladder? no — bullet has minimum cash-flow dispersion → LOWEST convexity for a given duration; the price falls less on rises and gains less on falls); BARBELL — extremes (3y+30y), maximum dispersion → HIGHEST convexity — wins when rates MOVE (large parallel swings, whichever way, beyond the carry the barbell pays) and when the curve flattens (short leg falls in value less than the long leg gains… check signs: flatten ⇒ long rates down ⇒ 30y leg rallies, 3y stable ⇒ barbell beats bullet); LADDER — even steps (auto-rolling of maturing rungs, reinvestment discipline, the 'default' for uncertain managers; liquidity of near rungs). Return decomposition: total = coupon income + ROLLOVER (a bond 'rolls down' an upward-sloping curve: as maturity shortens, yield declines, price rises — the roll-down return is the slope itself paid in capital gain) + PRICE CHANGE from yield shifts. Riding the curve: buy the 5y when the curve is steep and flat-to-down expectations prevail; earn the 5y coupon + roll-down to the 4y yield as time passes and (assuming no shifts) sell — the trade profits from the SLOPE, not the direction, and dies when the curve re-prices upward at the short end (2022 lesson); it implicitly borrows the roll and owns a short-rate risk if the shift comes early. Exam synthesis: choose shape by a VIEW — barbell (movement/flattening), bullet (directional at your point), ladder (no view, liquidity, reinvestment), and state the convexity argument — 'barbell needs a bigger yield give-up than bullet to hedge the same duration, buying insurance' — that's the marks.

keyPoints: Shape is a view, not a taste

questions.q: Explain duration-gap management for a bank with short liabilities and long fixed-rate assets; quantify the equity impact of a +1% rate move given DA=4.5 (on 900 crore assets) and DL=1.0 (on 850 crore liabilities).
questions.ans: ΔE ≈ −[DA·A − DL·L·(?) ]Δy: use ΔE = −(DA·A − DL·L)×Δy/(1+y) (or with 1+y adjusted). Here: DA·A = 4.5×900 = 4050; DL·L = 850; gap = 3200 crore-years; Δy=1% ⇒ equity change ≈ −32 crore (÷1+y if modified). Equity ERODES — classic asset-sensitive bank. Management levers: shorten asset duration (floating loans, securitise long fixed), lengthen liability duration (long CDs, retail sticky deposits treated as long due to low repricing beta), pay-fixed IRS/futures for the gap, or caps (asset-side protection for rate-rise fears) + limits via modified-duration gap and key-rate buckets; note convexity mismatch (mortgage-like prepayment shortens effective duration when rates fall — negative convexity risk).

questions.q: Define interest-rate risk in the banking book (IRRBB). Explain the repricing gap and duration-gap measures, their limitations, and the two earnings-vs-value dimensions the board must set limits on.
questions.ans: IRRBB = the risk that rate movements change the banking book's earnings or economic value — from repricing mismatches, yield-curve movements (non-parallel), basis (MCLR vs T-bill vs SOFR-linked loans moving differently), embedded options (prepayable loans, callable deposits, the borrower's free call in fixed-rate mortgages) and customer behaviour optionality (premature deposit breaks in a rate-rise rally — the repricing gap assumes contract dates, behaviour rewrites them). Measure 1 — REPRICING GAP (maturity buckets): GAPᵢ = RSAᵢ − RSLᵢ; ΔNII ≈ GAP × Δr bucket-weighted — earnings view, but blind to when the rate change hits (a 12-month horizon vs a 2-year gap mismatch), and it books gap-positive banks as 'safe' when they're actually just short-duration. Measure 2 — DURATION GAP (EVE view): D_gap = D_A − (L/A)D_L; ΔE/E ≈ −D_gap×Δy/(1+y) — economic-value sensitivity; limitation: small-yield parallel assumption, convexity ignored (prepayable assets flip negative convexity when rates fall — the gap lies precisely at turns), and market-value-vs-book-value framing (EVE on market rates, NII on accounting). The board's twin limits (the structure): (i) EARNINGS at risk: NII ±X% after +200/−200 bps shocks over 12 months (protect P&L, dividends, covenants); (ii) ECONOMIC VALUE at risk: EVE fall under six prescribed RBI-style parallel/non-parallel scenarios as % of capital (Basel's IRRBB standard — the 15%-of-Tier-1 style guardrail; cap the exposure, not the view); and governance adds behavioural-model validation (deposit-stickiness and prepayment curves audited separately — the model risk is where the true risk lives), plus basis-scenario add-ons. Close with the trap: a bank perfectly matched on gap can be un-hedged on basis (MCLR deposits vs CRR-linked advances) and short the options it sold (rate-cut prepays) — measures see the schedule, boards must see the behaviour.

keyPoints: Negative convexity breaks it at turns

questions.q: What does REDINGTON immunisation of a liability portfolio require, and what does it NOT protect against?
questions.ans: State the conditions (2): duration (present-value timing) matched so the first-order rate effect nets to zero; convexity of assets exceeds convexity of liabilities (with the dispersion condition for Redington). Explain the mechanics (1-2): small parallel shifts leave the surplus roughly unchanged to first order; the convexity advantage makes large moves net positive. Name the limits (2): immunises only PARALLEL shifts - key-rate and steepening changes break it; rebalancing is required as durations decay at different speeds; default, liquidity and embedded-option risks are ignored. Conclude (1): immunisation buys insensitivity to small parallel moves, not immunity to the yield curve, the market, or time.
questions.scheme: Redington conditions: D_A=D_L, C_A>C_L, PV_A>=PV_L; surplus insensitive to a small parallel shift; needs periodic rebalancing; fails on non-parallel shifts, embedded options, defaults.
keyPoints: parallel shifts only - key-rate risk remains

questions.q: For a growing but unlisted specialty-chemicals company, compare DCF and comparable-multiple valuation — sources of bias in each, and how a good report blends them (including the control/minority and liquidity adjustments).
questions.ans: DCF: intrinsic — cash-flow driven; biases: g beyond competitive decay, terminal dominance (>70% of value), WACC false precision, forecast optimism, missing synergy vs standalone discipline. Multiples: relative — market-sentiment anchored; biases: comparables selection (size, leverage, cycle-phase), cycle-window choice (peak EBITDA), net-debt mapping, no cash-flow check. Blending: football-field of methods (DCF + EV/EBITDA + P/E + P/B for asset-heavy); triangulate on drivers: growth vs margin vs risk; adjustments: control premium (majority stakes trade above market), minority discount and illiquidity discount for unlisted stakes (or DLOM), key-person discount, working-capital peg and net-debt normalisation, ESG/regulatory tail-risk haircut; document range and the weights, and let the negotiation anchor to the bridge (what changes value).

questions.q: Explain how due-diligence findings convert a headline valuation into a negotiated price in an Indian deal: quality-of-earnings adjustments, the SPA mechanisms that carry them, and what good diligence says about the price you should walk away from.
questions.ans: Price = value + adjustments + risk allocation, and diligence IS the adjustment finder. Quality of earnings (the engine): normalise run-rate EBITDA — add back promoter perks and above-market related-party salaries, strip one-off gains, annualise partial-year contracts (the 'last-12-months flattering the exit'), and check revenue recognition (percentage-of-completion over-runs on EPC, bill-and-hold, channel-stuffing before quarter-ends, the Indian classic). Findings convert into PRICE through SPA machinery: (i) the working-capital peg (over-target receivables = cash the seller is shipping with the business — price falls, peg rises); (ii) net-debt-like items discovered (unbooked gratuity, statutory dues, unpaid PF, GST demands, litigation provisions — deducted like quasi-debt; 'debt-like' schedule negotiation is the real battlefield); (iii) one-off capex or maintenance gaps (deferred maintenance = priced as a deduction, not a multiple); (iv) earn-outs and escrows where diligence found UNCERTAINTY (a revenue-linked earn-out buys the contested growth back for the seller's risk; escrow = the quantified tail priced into a blocked account). The walk-away layer: when findings show earnings QUALITY dependence (customer concentration with a renewal date before close, a licence in litigation), the answer is not a haircut but a deal-structure refusal — pay for what you can diligence, price the tail in contingencies, or lower the multiple; never 'fix' a broken business case with a bigger synergy note. Exam conclusion: a good diligence report is a bridge schedule, not a memo — every finding lands on a line that moves price, peg, indemnity or walk — the four P's: price, paper (SPA), payments (escrow), pass.

questions.q: Explain the logic of a leveraged buyout: who pays what at entry, what carries the debt, how value is created during hold, and how the exit repays it. Then give two reasons an LBO can fail.
questions.ans: Entry: a financial sponsor buys a CONTROL stake funded 60-75% with debt — term loans and bonds secured against the TARGET's own assets and cash flows (leverage sits on the company, serviced by its future cash; the seller receives price paid largely by the small sponsor equity cheque). Discipline that makes it work: (i) covenants force cash discipline; (ii) interest is tax-deductible — the shield converts to cash that repays principal (deleveraging is the value engine); (iii) sponsor equity is the thin first-loss band, amplifying IRR both ways. Hold: value creation = EBITDA growth (opex programmes, bolt-ons), multiple expansion (buy low, sell high — cyclical, not controllable), and DEBT PAYDOWN from free cash flow (the near-certain driver: equity at exit = EV minus net debt, so each rupee of amortisation is a rupee of equity). Exit: IPO or strategic re-sale judged on the same multiple yardstick as entry — the exit multiple is the round-trip risk. Failure modes: (1) leverage beyond cash-flow capacity — a cyclical EBITDA dip turns fixed charges into a covenant crisis and the equity pours in to fund a zombie; (2) peak-cycle entry — overpaying a top-of-cycle multiple means debt not repaid AND a compressed exit multiple, the double whammy. Honest third: sponsors cannot rely on synergies the way strategics do, so the operating plan must beat the incumbent — the plan is the real hedge.

keyPoints: Seller paid from levered EV; company carries the debt

questions.q: Explain why standalone value, equity (fair) value and investment value differ in an acquisition price, and how synergy, control premium and DLOM each map to those bases.
questions.ans: Standalone (fair, to a minority buyer on market terms) ≈ market value; investment value = worth to THIS buyer incl. synergies and control benefits — the gap is what funds the premium. Control premium: buyer pays above market for the power to reprice the target's cash flows (restructure, change payout, sell assets) — the premium's ceiling = PV of controllable synergies minus competition; synergy must be MEASURABLE (cost cuts have higher probability than revenue deals) and time-phased (delayed = discounted); overpaying = winner's curse in auctions (common-value). DLOM (minority/illiquid stake): the discount for a buyer without control or easy exit — in reverse, the minority discount. The price bridge: fair value + PV(synergy to buyer) − value of risks = maximum price; premium split determines the deal's 'accretion to whom'.

questions.topic: Scheme of arrangement versus other routes
questions.q: A promoter wants to merge two group companies. Compare the scheme of arrangement route with a takeover-offer route and a slump sale, on process, timelines, minority protection, and tax.
questions.ans: Scheme of arrangement (s.230–234 NCLT route): a court-sanctioned compromise — board proposal, NCLT admission, directions for a meeting (regulator notices: SEBI, RBI, stock exchanges), majority test (¾ value + ½ number... careful: 75% in value AND majority in number of each class), then NCLT sanction with the fairness of valuation (registered valuer report) reviewed, filed with RoC — EFFECTIVE ON SANCTION: vests assets by operation of law, binds dissenters, needs no separate stamp on each asset transfer (state stamp-duty nuances still apply to the instrument). Timelines: 6–12 months; cost: legal + court + notice machinery; minority protection: the class meeting and 75% test, plus an OFD for delisting-like effects and a fairness letter — the dissenting minority is BOUND, which is both the power and the danger. Takeover route (acquire shares, then squeeze): SEBI SAST open offer at a regulated price, acquires 90% to use the squeeze-out (s.236: purchase at a price by majority of the minority... the valuation-fairness safety), or delist via the majority-out (2024 framework: 75–90% routes) — heavier regulation (open-offer price discovery), faster in simple cases, but leaves the target's separate legal identity unless followed by a scheme anyway; asset-by-asset transfer without either (business purchase): stamp duty per state, third-party consents (licenses don't move!), contracts re-sign — the slow death of deal certainty. Slump sale (whole-business transfer for consideration, no consideration allocated): income-tax neutral-ish for the buyer's step-up (no step-up — the buyer inherits written-down values), gain to seller taxed as capital (short/long by holding), no court, consents still needed for licences/contracts — quick, clean on title only if counterparties cooperate. For a merger of group companies, the scheme wins on universality (all assets/contracts move by order; court's sanction = a defence of fairness) and loses on timeline; the answer should also flag the NCLT's scrutiny of the VALUATION (registered valuer, not the bank's comfort letter) — the classic point where 'scheme = cheap' dies.

keyPoints: Open offer + squeeze = costlier, separate identity persists
